candidates.draft_body:

'And they made for themselves molten images, and they worshipped each the idol the molten image which they had made for themselves, and they began to make graven images and unclean simulacra' — Jubilees traces the cascade of post-Babel apostasy through Serug's generation, presenting idolatry not as a single fall but as a slow societal drift. Tewahedo catechesis (Andəmta on Genesis 11) inherits this gradualist diagnosis: sin is taught, learned, and inherited within communities, so the antidote — Abram's break, then Sinai, then Christ's gathered ecclesia — likewise advances by community-formation, not isolated individual conversion.

candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And Serug grew up and dwelt in Ur of the Chaldees, near to the father of his wife's mother, and he worshipped idols' — Jubilees marks the precise generation in which the rot becomes nominal: Abram's great-grandfather Serug actively serves the idols of his in-laws. The Tewahedo Andəmta exegesis on Abram's election reads this verse as proof that elective grace stands against inherited line: God draws Abram from a pedigree of idolators, not from an unbroken righteous succession — a key anti-Pelagian and anti-genealogical-merit anchor in Tewahedo soteriology.

candidates.draft_body:

'And the child began to understand the errors of the earth that all went astray after graven images and after uncleanness, and his father taught him writing, and he was two weeks of years old, and he separated himself from his father, that he might not worship idols with him' — young Abram rejects his father's idolatry. Tewahedo missiological tradition cites this verse as the canonical witness that conversion-from-idolatry CAN happen even within a thoroughly pagan household — a foundational warrant for evangelism into traditional-religious contexts.

candidates.source_attribution: Jubilees 11:18 (Abraham cycle (11:18)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And in the third week of that jubilee the unclean ravens came and devoured the seed which had been sown in the earth in order to destroy the earth' — Jubilees portrays the ravens as Mastema's instruments sent to ruin the agricultural blessing. Tewahedo readers see in the boy-Abram who drives away the ravens (11:19-21) the prototype of the priest who guards the offered seed; the Tewahedo blessing of the fields and the kahn (priestly) intercession against locust and crop-loss draw their canonical warrant from this passage. Abram is presented as priest-king before Mosaic ordination — anchoring the Tewahedo doctrine of universal pre-Mosaic priesthood from which the kǝhnät descends.
